intro: Rachmaninoff, Stokowski and the Philadelphia Orchestra recorded this opening of the Adagio on 10 April 1929. HMV D.B. 1334 preserves its first 78-rpm side; the later middle section, cadenza and return are not included here.
question: How do the broad melody and the piano’s smaller notes share the same pulse?

cues.title: The Adagio’s first side
cues.text: This is the slow movement’s first 78-rpm side, labelled No. 4 in the concerto’s sequence. Compare only its opening with Richter: the later cadenza and the returning song lie on other sides, not beyond an artificial join in this file.
cues.evidence: The HMV label identifies “2nd Movement–Adagio sostenuto (1st Record)” and No. 4; DAHR identifies CVE-48966 as part 4. https://adp.library.ucsb.edu/index.php/matrix/refer/800022752
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: The opening swell recedes
cues.text: After the opening rise, the recorded sound withdraws over a longer stretch. Listen for the difference between a sustained phrase and the smaller notes moving beneath it, without assuming that quieter sound means a slower pulse.
cues.evidence: cache/analysis/rachmaninoff-concerto-2-adagio-rachmaninoff-1929-side1.txt: relative level reaches −5.2 dB at 0:15, falls to −12.9 at 0:25 and −18.0 at 0:45; novelty peaks at 0:22 and 0:28. This identifies a broad withdrawal, not individual instrumental entrances or a measured tempo change.

cues.title: The slow movement’s master
cues.text: The first Adagio side comes from the same 10 April 1929 Philadelphia session as the concerto’s opening. Its master is CVE-48966, take 1. The label’s No. 4 counts its place in the concerto’s disc sequence, not a fourth movement.
cues.evidence: DAHR identifies Part 4, Second movement: Adagio sostenuto, recorded at the Academy of Music on 10 April 1929; take 1 was issued on DB-1334. https://adp.library.ucsb.edu/index.php/matrix/refer/800022752

cues.title: Follow the whole phrase
cues.text: Across this stretch, the recorded level rises, falls and rises again. Follow the phrase through its quieter interval instead of treating every crest as a new beginning; then compare how Richter connects the corresponding notes.
cues.evidence: cache/analysis/rachmaninoff-concerto-2-adagio-rachmaninoff-1929-side1.txt: relative level moves from −17.7 dB at 1:25 to −12.2 at 1:35, −17.1 at 1:40 and −12.0 at 1:45. The cue describes this within-file contour and proposes a comparison, not a measured interpretation of phrasing.

cues.title: Four styli, one chosen transfer
cues.text: George Blood’s engineers transferred the disc with four styli. The selected file uses a 3.3-mil truncated-conical stylus and turnover equalisation of 500.0. These transfer decisions affect the balance of music and surface noise; they are not instructions in Rachmaninoff’s score.
cues.evidence: The item description documents four stylus transfers; the preferred FLAC comment identifies the selected 3.3-mil stylus and turnover setting. https://archive.org/details/78_concerto-no-2-in-c-minor-op-18-2nd-movement-1st-record_sergei-rachmaninoff-and_gbia7026859b

cues.title: Another rise within the side
cues.text: A later swell grows within the material preserved on this side. Compare its rise and retreat with the opening swell, keeping the long line in view rather than judging the passage by the number of audible attacks.
cues.evidence: cache/analysis/rachmaninoff-concerto-2-adagio-rachmaninoff-1929-side1.txt: novelty at 2:20 precedes a rise from −17.5 dB at 2:25 to −12.5 at 2:35, followed by a fall to −16.5 at 2:50. Surface noise compromises attack counts, which are not published as musical measurements.

cues.title: A side of a larger work
cues.text: HMV paired this Adagio opening with the first movement’s third side on D.B. 1334. The Archive dates that issue to November 1929. The disc’s coupling explains the break in the surviving file; it does not turn the opening song into a self-contained slow movement.
cues.evidence: The Archive’s other-side link identifies the first movement’s third record; metadata.date is 1929-11. DAHR lists CVE-48965 and CVE-48966 on DB-1334. https://adp.library.ucsb.edu/index.php/objects/refer/173510

quote.text: I feel like a ghost wandering in a world grown alien. I cannot cast out the old way of writing, and I cannot acquire the new.
quote.source: Interview with Leonard Liebling, The Musical Courier, 1939

composer.background:
Rachmaninoff learnt the sound of Russian worship before he learnt orchestration. His grandmother took him to Orthodox services, where unaccompanied voices and bells occupied different parts of the ceremony: chant inside the church, metal sounding above and outside it. His music repeatedly brings the two together. A melody moves in narrow steps while bass notes toll beneath it; a chord is struck again before its previous resonance has died. The C♯ minor Prelude, the Second Piano Concerto and The Bells make this audible without requiring an actual church bell. The All-Night Vigil removes the instruments altogether, leaving a choir to produce both the sustained line and the accumulating weight of the harmony.

Born into a landowning family in 1873, he spent his early childhood at Oneg, near Novgorod. His father’s financial failures brought the sale of the estates and a move to St Petersburg. Rachmaninoff entered its Conservatory in 1883, but his general schoolwork deteriorated; his parents separated, and his sister Sofia died of diphtheria. In 1885 his cousin Alexander Siloti recommended a transfer to Moscow and the supervision of Nikolai Zverev. The move exchanged a disorganised household for one in which practice, meals and attendance at concerts were regulated by a piano teacher.
composer.epithet: A composer-pianist who built long melodies over tolling basses, and carried Russian chant into the concertos and dances of his American exile.
